lesson.title: Church Modes
lesson.summary: Seven scales use the notes of the white keys from different starting points; each has its own color.

section.title: Seven modes on the white keys
section.p: Play a scale on the white keys of the piano, starting from each of the seven notes in turn. Each starting note gives a different order of whole steps and half steps, and so a different mode:

list.li: Ionian, from C: the same as the major scale.
Aeolian, from A: the same as the natural minor scale.

figure.staff: D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 B4 C5 D5
figure.caption: The Dorian mode on D: white keys from D to D.

section.p: Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian and Mixolydian are the church modes of medieval and Renaissance music, each with its final on D, E, F or G. In 1547 the Swiss theorist Heinrich Glarean added Ionian and Aeolian. Locrian, whose fifth above the final is diminished, remained a theoretical possibility and is still rarely used. Today the modes are heard in folk music, jazz, film music and much music of the twentieth century.

check.prompt: Which mode do the white keys form from G to G?
check.explanation: From C, the white-key modes are Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian and Locrian. G is the fifth note, so it gives Mixolydian. Lydian starts on F and Dorian on D.

section.title: Comparing modes with major and minor
section.p: Apart from Ionian and Aeolian, each mode differs from major or natural minor on the same tonic by one or two notes. These characteristic notes give the mode its color:

list.li: Lydian: major with a raised fourth degree.
Mixolydian: major with a lowered seventh degree.
Dorian: natural minor with a raised sixth degree.
Phrygian: natural minor with a lowered second degree.
Locrian: natural minor with a lowered second and fifth degree.

figure.staff: C4 D4 E4 *F#4 G4 A4 B4 C5 || C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 *Bb4 C5 ||
figure.caption: C Lydian with its raised fourth, F#, then C Mixolydian with its lowered seventh, Bb.

figure.staff: C4 D4 Eb4 F4 G4 *A4 Bb4 C5 || C4 *Db4 Eb4 F4 G4 Ab4 Bb4 C5 ||
figure.caption: C Dorian with its raised sixth, A, then C Phrygian with its lowered second, Db.

figure.staff: C4 *Db4 Eb4 F4 *Gb4 Ab4 Bb4 C5 ||
figure.caption: C Locrian: the lowered second, Db, and the lowered fifth, Gb, which makes the tonic triad diminished.

section.p: Ordered from brightest to darkest, the modes are Lydian, Ionian, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian and Locrian. Each mode in this order lowers one more degree of the one before: the fourth, then the seventh, the third, the sixth, the second and finally the fifth.

check.prompt: Which mode is natural minor with a raised sixth degree?
check.explanation: On D, natural minor has Bb and Dorian has B: the white keys from D. Phrygian lowers the second degree instead, and Mixolydian is a major mode.

section.title: Finding the notes of a mode
section.p: Every mode uses the notes of some major scale, starting from a different degree: Dorian from the second degree, Phrygian from the third, Lydian from the fourth, Mixolydian from the fifth, Aeolian from the sixth and Locrian from the seventh. This gives a quick way to find its notes and its key signature.

worked.title: Find the notes of a Mixolydian mode

step.p: Mixolydian starts on the fifth degree of a major scale. Which major key has A as its fifth degree? Count a fifth down from A: D.
D major has two sharps, F# and C#, so A Mixolydian has them too: A B C# D E F# G A.
Check with the characteristic note. A major has G#; Mixolydian lowers the seventh degree to G. The two methods agree.

figure.staff: A4 B4 C#5 D5 E5 F#5 *G5 A5

section.p: Music in a mode is written in two ways. Some editions use the key signature of the related major scale, as above; others use the signature of the major or minor key on the same tonic and add accidentals for the characteristic notes.

check.prompt: How many sharps does D Mixolydian have?
check.explanation: D is the fifth degree of G major, which has one sharp, F#. Compared with D major, Mixolydian lowers C# to C, leaving one sharp.

check.prompt: B Phrygian uses the notes of which major scale?
check.explanation: Phrygian starts on the third degree of a major scale. B is the third degree of G major, so B Phrygian has one sharp: B C D E F# G A B.

section.title: Hearing modes
section.p: To recognize a mode by ear, first decide whether its third is major or minor, then listen for the characteristic note:

list.li: Lydian: a major mode with a tritone above the tonic; it sounds bright and floating.
Mixolydian: a major mode without a leading tone. The seventh degree lies a whole step below the tonic, and the triad on the fifth degree is minor.
Dorian: a minor mode whose bright major sixth softens its darkness.
Phrygian: a minor mode with a half step from the tonic up to the second degree; it sounds dark and severe.
Locrian: its diminished tonic triad never sounds at rest.

check.prompt: Which of these modes has a half step between its first and second degrees?
check.explanation: Phrygian, the white keys from E, begins E–F: a half step. Dorian and Lydian begin with a whole step. Locrian, not among the options, also begins with a half step.

figure.staff: G4 A4 B4 C5 D5 E5 *F5 G5
figure.description: A scale of eight notes rising by step from the second line of the treble staff, without key signature or accidentals. The seventh note is highlighted.

check.explanation: The scale has a major third, G–B, so it is a major mode. Its seventh degree, F, lies a whole step below the tonic: G major would have F#. A major scale with a lowered seventh is Mixolydian.
